issues.legal_issue: An employer operating under an enforceable gratuity scheme that authorizes recovery of its dues may deduct assessed charges for an employee’s unauthorized retention of employer-provided housing from retirement gratuity.
material_facts: The employer was a statutory corporation whose regulations provided for recovery of its dues from gratuity without the employee’s consent.
After retirement, the employee was permitted to retain the employer-provided accommodation for a limited period and was told that charges would be imposed if he did not vacate by the deadline.

The employee’s request for an extension was rejected on grounds including the accommodation needs of other employees, but he continued to occupy the premises after the permitted period despite notice of the charges.
Eviction proceedings were initiated, and the employee vacated only after giving an undertaking in those proceedings.
The employer assessed charges for the unauthorized occupation and deducted them from the gratuity payable.
issues.conclusion: The employer was entitled under its regulations to recover the charges from the employee’s gratuity, and the deduction was not unlawful.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(1) of the Oil and Natural Gas Commission Act, 1959 authorized regulations that the Constitution Bench in Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram Sardar Singh Raghuvanshi held to be statutory and enforceable. Regulation 5 of the Oil and Natural Gas Commission (Death, Retirement and Terminal Gratuity) Regulations, 1969 expressly permitted recovery of the Commission’s dues from gratuity without consent. Jarnail Singh v. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs supports adjustment of dues against retirement gratuity where the governing rules authorize it, and Wazir Chand v. Union of India supports recovery of charges for unauthorized occupation from retirement benefits. R. Kapur v. Director of Inspection and Gorakhpur University v. Shilla Prasad Nagendra were distinguishable because the relevant dues there were pending or disputed, or the employer’s conduct otherwise made recovery unreasonable.

predicates.gratuity_deduction_dispute: The proceeding concerns an employer’s deduction of a claimed debt from retirement gratuity.
predicates.binding_gratuity_scheme_authorizes_recov: The employer is governed by an enforceable gratuity scheme that permits its dues to be recovered from gratuity without the employee’s consent.
predicates.occupancy_charges_are_assessed_as_due: The employer assesses charges as payable for the employee’s occupation of employer-provided accommodation beyond the permitted period.
predicates.employee_remains_after_permission_expire: The employee continues occupying the accommodation after permission ends despite being told to vacate and warned of charges.

issues.definition: When a gratuity-deduction dispute involves an enforceable scheme authorizing recovery, assessed occupancy charges, and continued occupation after permission expires despite notice, the employer may deduct those charges from gratuity.

issues.legal_issue: An employee whose wages exceed the applicable employee-coverage limit at retirement is not covered by the gratuity legislation then in force where a later amendment removing that limit does not apply retrospectively.
material_facts: At the time of the employee’s retirement, the statutory definition of employee limited coverage to persons whose monthly wages did not exceed the then-applicable ceiling.
The employee’s monthly salary exceeded that ceiling.
The ceiling was removed by a later amendment, which was not retrospective.
issues.conclusion: The employee was not covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 as it applied at the time of retirement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(e) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, as it stood at the relevant time, confined the definition of employee by a monthly-wage ceiling. The later amendment removing that ceiling was not retrospective. Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners’ Association and Anr. supports determining an employee’s entitlement by the law applicable at retirement, rather than by a later change.

predicates.gratuity_coverage_case: The proceeding requires a determination of whether an employee is covered by a general statutory gratuity scheme.
predicates.employee_wages_exceed_applicable_coverag: The employee’s wages at retirement exceed the coverage limit then in force for the relevant class of employees.
predicates.later_removal_of_limit_is_not_retroactiv: A later change removes the wage limit but does not apply to earlier retirements.

issues.definition: If a gratuity-coverage case concerns an employee whose wages at retirement exceeded the then-applicable limit and the later removal of that limit is not retrospective, the employee is not covered by that gratuity legislation.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court should not grant discretionary writ relief to prevent recovery of charges for unauthorized occupation of employer-provided housing where the employee was given a reasonable time to vacate, was refused an extension on relevant grounds, received notice of the consequences, and continued to occupy the accommodation.
material_facts: The proceeding was a writ petition challenging the deduction of charges from retirement benefits.
The employee had been allowed a period after retirement to vacate employer-provided accommodation.
The employer considered and rejected the employee’s request for further retention on grounds that included the need to provide accommodation to other employees.
The employer warned that continued occupation would result in penal charges, but the employee remained in occupation and the employer initiated eviction proceedings.
The employer had returned possession of a separate residence belonging to the employee, which had been leased to the employer.
The Court found no basis in the circumstances for treating the employer’s action as arbitrary or unreasonable or for granting equitable relief.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in exercising its extraordinary and equitable jurisdiction to grant relief, and its order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 of the Constitution confers discretionary, equitable jurisdiction rather than appellate jurisdiction for correcting every legal error. G. Veerappa Pillai v. Raman & Raman Ltd. describes writ intervention in grave cases such as jurisdictional excess, breach of natural justice, or manifest injustice. Sangram Singh v. Election Commissioner states that writ jurisdiction should not be used to correct errors that do not occasion substantial injustice. The Court distinguished circumstances involving disputed dues, acquiescence, or hostile discrimination, as discussed in R. Kapur v. Director of Inspection and Gorakhpur University v. Shilla Prasad Nagendra.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_recovery_from_retirement_benefits and reasonable_vacate_period_was_given and extension_was_rejected_on_relevant_grounds and employee_continued_after_warning and employer_action_was_not_arbitrary_or_discriminatory

predicates.writ_challenge_to_recovery_from_retireme: The proceeding is a writ challenge to an employer’s recovery of charges from retirement benefits.
predicates.reasonable_vacate_period_was_given: The employer allowed the former employee a period after employment ended to vacate the accommodation.
predicates.extension_was_rejected_on_relevant_groun: The employer considered a request for further occupancy and rejected it for grounds connected to legitimate accommodation or operational needs.
predicates.employee_continued_after_warning: The former employee remained in the accommodation after being warned that continued occupation would have financial consequences.
predicates.employer_action_was_not_arbitrary_or_dis: The employer applied its position on grounds that were not arbitrary or discriminatory.

issues.definition: In a writ challenge to recovery from retirement benefits, where a reasonable time to vacate was given, an extension was reasonably refused, the former employee stayed after warning, and the employer acted without arbitrariness or discrimination, writ relief against recovery should be denied.
